articles.title: Dangerous escalation
articles.content: JUST weeks after its formation, theMakkah Joint Defence Agreementfaces its first challenge: theescalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi militia. The rebel group has struck Saudi air bases andkey oil facilitieswith missiles and drones, while the kingdom has intensified air strikes on Houthi-held areas in Yemen. The Houthis have also targeted Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea. The escalation began in mid-July, when the Houthisformally declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabiaand began hitting Saudi-flagged shipping, after Yemeni government forces attacked a flight from Iran at Sana’a airport. The Houthis have been fighting Yemen’s internationally recognised government since 2014. The violence subsided after the warring sides reached an internationally brokered ceasefire in 2022, but flared up again after the July incident when the militia broke the truce, declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea and began attacking Saudi vessels. Its ultimate aim is to drive Saudi Arabia out of Yemen and take full control of the territory. This latest escalation has widened the conflict in West Asia, even as America’s war with Iran grinds on with no end in sight. With the fighting now threatening Saudi Arabia directly, will the kingdom invoke the alliance’s mutual defence clause — the one that treats an attack on one member as an attack on all members? The danger of a wider conflagration engulfing the entire region carries serious implications for the rest of the world. The Houthis, who already hold much of Yemen, have seized a strategic island in a lightning offensive against government forces, giving them complete control of Bab al-Mandeb — the key marine chokepoint through which 12 per cent of the world’s trade passes. They now control 90 per cent of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline. The Houthi leadership says it is not seeking to block all commercial shipping in the Red Sea, only Saudi-linked vessels. But the heightening tension is likely to keep other ships away. With the Strait of Hormuz virtually blocked, the situation is explosive. Global energy markets, already reeling from the six-month conflict between US-Israel and Iran, are bracing for further shock. Saudi Arabia, which had stayed out of the Iran war, now risks being drawn into a wider conflict. These actions by a militia widely seen as aligned with Iran have opened a new front in the conflict. They have coincided with a drone attack, apparently launched from Iraq by allegedly another Iran-linked militia, that forced temporary closure of the East-West oil pipeline crossing Saudi Arabia. Together, the attacks have disrupted Saudi oil exports. It is widely accepted that Iran backs the Houthis, though the group also operates independently of Tehran. The attacks on Saudi Arabia are certainly not in Iran’s interest while it is engaged in an existential war with the US — the fallout is already visible. Saudi Arabia, which had so far kept itself out of the Iran war, is now in danger of being drawn into a wider regional conflict. Although Iran hasdistanced itself from the attacks on Saudi oil infrastructureby the two militias, the incidents have heightened tensions between Riyadh and Tehran. Following the attacks, talks between Iran and the Gulf states aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz werepostponed. It would have been the first meeting between Iran and the main GCC member states in two years; the meeting, to be held in Oman, was part of an effort to find a regional solution allowing free passage through the critical waterway. The latest flare-up has thwarted that effort. As the fighting spreads, Saudi Arabia finds itself on the front line. In the latest turn, the kingdom reportedlysought American military help, only to be turned down by President Donald Trump, who said the Houthis had assured him they did not want to expand the conflict. The development has given an intriguing twist to the conflict. Trump’s response is said to be driven by his frustration with the kingdom for failing to actively support his war against Iran. America and Israel have carried out missile strikes against the Houthis in the past over their support for the Palestinian resistance. But there is also the question of whether US intervention in the Saudi-Houthi conflict will help stabilise a situation for which Washington is itself responsible. The growing tension between Iran and Saudi Arabia will only serve the US agenda in the region. So far, Saudi Arabia has not formally invoked the Makkah defence alliance clause, which would require Pakistan and Turkiye to come to its defence if it is attacked. But consultations are under way as the conflict spreads. Diplomatic efforts to halt the Houthis’ escalatory moves are still continuing. Reportedly, Pakistan’s military chief and the Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan both spoke to Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. Pakistan is also believed to have conveyed a Saudi message urging Iran to rein in the Houthis, and reminded Tehran of Islamabad’s own pact commitment to Riyadh. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif recentlysaidthat unprovoked aggression against the kingdom, or a spillover into it, would make the pact operational — “there should be no doubt about that”. Earlier, in April 2026, Saudi Arabia’s defence ministry announced that a Pakistani military contingent had arrived at King Abdulaziz Air Base, with fighter and support aircraft, under abilateral defence pact signed in September 2025. Following Khawaja Asif’s remarks, however, the Foreign Office spokespersonsaid, “I don’t think we should be discussing this topic in the context of its operationalisation”. The situation remains dangerous for both Pakistan and the larger region, and the widening conflict could suck in even those countries that have kept out of the Iran war and have been trying to help broker a negotiated end to it. Pakistan needs to tread a more cautious path in a conflict that could prove disastrous for the country. It’s a perilous escalation that needs to be resolved through negotiations rather than war.
articles.author: Zahid Hussain

articles.title: Karachi: how much dirtier?
articles.content: AS they say everything comes at a cost — and so does Karachi’srankingas one of the least liveable cities. Karachi has slipped from the seventh least liveable city in 2021 to the fourth least liveable one in 2026. It ranks 170th among the 173 cities surveyed by the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU). This decline has come despite enormous spending by the Sindh government — estimated at around Rs126 billion in these five years alone — to garbage-collection contractors. Since 2017, including the current year’s allocation, spending on garbage collection and street sweeping is estimated to exceed Rs190bn, with an estimated Rs160-170bn spent in the name of Karachi alone. No other initiative has received such generous provincial financing over the past decade — not the BRT Red Line, the BRT Yellow Line, the K-IV water supply project, the Safe City project, Karachi’s road network, not even the Right Bank Outfall Drain, which is critical to rural Sindh’s economy. When the EIU measures liveability, environmental quality is only one of five major criteria, with cleanliness forming a sub-component. However, on Numbeo’s global pollution index, Karachi continues to rank as one of the world’s most polluted cities with a pollution index score of 89.5/100. This index evaluates air quality, drinking water availability, garbage disposal, cleanliness, water pollution, noise and light pollution, green spaces, and overall comfort. Across all these metrics, garbage disposal has remained the poorest performer despite billions being spent by the Sindh Solid Waste Management Board (SSWMB) under the chief minister’s chairmanship. In 2016, the Sindh government took over the municipal functions of garbage collection and street sweeping — previously managed by the KMC and union councils — and outsourced them to foreign firms. The contracts covered door-to-door collection, sweeping of streets, lanes, medians, footpaths and open spaces, transportation to transfer stations and landfills, provision of bins and compactors, deployment of sanitary workers, and GPS-based monitoring. Initially introduced across Karachi’s districts, the outsourcing model was later extended to Hyderabad, Sukkur and Larkana. The city’s dismal ranking on the liveability and pollution indexes reflects a crisis of governance more than a shortage of funds. The system was designed around a simple principle: garbage should not remain on the ground. Mini-trucks were to collect waste door to door and from designated bins, feed it into compactors at district collection centres, and ensure its transportation to landfill sites the same day. Uncollected areas, roadside garbage, failure to deploy prescribed staff or machinery, and other performance lapses attracted financial penalties. Vehicles were to be GPS-tracked, while manual sweeping supplemented mechanical cleaning. A command-and-control system linked to the SSWMB headquarters was to monitor fleet movements; an independent firm was to verify the contractors’ performance; and complaints were to be resolved within eight hours. Going by these performance indicators — and an estimated public-sector price tag approaching Rs170bn for the city over the period — Karachi should have become one of the cleanest cities in the region during the past decade. Yet the reality across much of the city is different. Open plots continue to serve as informal garbage dumps. Door-to-door collection remains patchy or is altogether absent in many localities. Waste continues to accumulate along the roads, open spaces and drains. Elected representatives themselves frequently complain about inadequate responsiveness by solid-waste contractors. Karachi continues to be ranked as one of the dirtiest cities all these 10 years. A review of these contracts against the ground realities over the past decade suggests that strict enforcement of the built-in penalty clauses should have driven non-compliant contractors into bankruptcy. The obvious question is: how have contractors been able to operate with such visible gaps between contractual obligations and conditions on the ground? The answer lies in two major contract and statutory violations by the provincial administration itself. First, the Sindh government has failed to hire an independent consulting firm for third-party verification since 2017, effectively granting contractors a decade-long exemption from performance audits. Second, the government has bypassed Section 14(3) of the Sindh Solid Waste Management Act, 2021, which states: “The executive directors of the board shall be appointed by the chief minister either from cadre service officers working under the control of government having relevant professional qualification and experience or from private sector through a competitive process possessing the requisite qualifications and experience of the post.” Despite managing contracts valued at Rs30-40bn, a key oversight position, such as director monitoring and evaluation, has been filled by an officer from the Benazir Income Support Programme. Compounding the issue is the lack of parliamentary oversight. Reports from the Auditor General of Pakistan from 2018 through 2025 have repeatedly highlighted losses of billions of rupees by the SSWMB due to payments made without third-party verification, uncollected penalties, inadequate staffing, and overpayments. Yet, no effective corrective action has been taken all these years. The State of Governance in Pakistan, 2023, based on a nationwide household survey by TDEA/ Fafen, found 65 per cent of Karachi respondents to be dissatisfied with garbage disposal services, while another 22pc had no service available in their locality. So, 87pc of Karachi households surveyed were either dissatisfied with garbage disposal or had no service — a remarkable outcome after years of outsourcing and billions of rupees spent on solid-waste management. After chairing the board for seven years, starting in 2014, the chief minister transferred the steering committee to the local government minister in 2021, and operational supervision was handed to the mayor of Karachi in 2024. However, meaningful coordination with elected town chairmen and union councils to hold contractors accountable remains absent. In fact, despite their poor performance, SSWMB contractors were rewarded with a 42pc increase in payment, raising their annual bill from Rs28.3bn in 2024-25 to Rs40.3bn in 2025-26. Like many of Karachi’s challenges, the real bottleneck has not been the shortage of funds for the Sindh government, but poor governance and lack of accountability. With the country’s economic engine ranking among the lowest on the liveability index and among the highest on the pollution index, all our aspirations for the country’s progress will remain a pipe dream. The writer is former federal secretary, caretaker provincial minister and currently chairman, Policy Research and Advisory Council.
articles.author: Mohammad Younus Dagha

articles.title: Artificial audacity
articles.content: AMID a rising tide of warnings about the grave risks posed by unregulated artificial intelligence, including from leading figures in the American tech industry, the leader of an increasingly unfree world is typically insouciant. “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs,” Donald Trump declared in a Truth Social post this week, “is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the USA has that, in spades!” Surely, that was an unnecessary reminder. After all, hardly anyone could be unaware of what that super-intelligence in the glittering Oval Office hath wrought, and perhaps the incorrigible optimists among us can still cling to the vague hope that his efforts will succeed in dismantling the American empire without irreparably damaging all life on earth. “Concerning AI, when, in the History of Business, did anyone see the Leaders of an Industry call for Regulation that, strongly implemented, will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy?” the same high-IQ personality wonders in a longer post. As a six-times veteran, Trump knows a thing or two about bankruptcies but, either through ignorance or malice, misinterprets the existential worries of Anthropic and OpenAI executives, whose concerns may well be selfish rather than selflessly humanitarian. They have witnessed how AI ‘agents’ can ‘decide’ to pursue goals that involve no human agency, and even worked out strategies for deceiving their ‘controllers’. It should come as no surprise that the self-proclaimed ‘Hoax Buster’ compares the concerns over AI to the barely audible worries about global heating, regardless of the mounting evidence from Nepal to Europe. “The people that say AI is going to destroy the World, and that Data Centres are bad for your neighbourhood, are the same people that said, just a short time ago, that the World would be extinguished by ‘Climate Change’. That HOAX never worked out for them, and now they are on to the next one… .” AI’s use as a military tactic indicates its destructive powers. Climate change has been wreaking havoc worldwide for a long time, but almost as soon as Trump returned to the White House, most fossil fuel firms abandoned all pretence of leaning towards green ventures and embraced the ‘drill, baby, drill’ imperative. Perhaps the only country that has noticeably gone greener since the Trumpian blockages in the Strait of Hormuz is China, where the use of oil has substantially diminished. China is also a clear contender for supremacy in the AI race, which is one of the main reasons why constraints on advancement are anathema to the US cold warriors. The developers in China are also concerned about the future. Beijing has dismissed Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s warning that “a Chinese lead in AI would pose a grave danger for the US and the world” as “fearmongering”. China has widely deployed AI in functions ranging from mass surveillance to manufacturing, but at least Xi Jinping openly acknowledges the need for AI to “always remain under human control”. China’s state security minister, Chen Yixin, has noted the risks of “hostile forces” waging a “cognitive war” that would threaten “our political security, institutional security and ideological security”. It is perhaps somewhat ironic that China, with its open-source AI models, is more willing than the US to pursue internationally agreed constraints on the pursuit of a technology that potentially offers innumerable benefits to humankind in a wide range of spheres, but is also capable of eradicating humanity. Its deployment as a military option from Israel and the US to Russia and Ukraine is an indicator of its destructive capacity. Were AI agents to conclude that human beings were merely standing in the way of their autonomously conceived goals, it might seem logical to eliminate the impediment. And given the extent to which we, knowingly or otherwise, rely on technology for our survival, that aim wouldn’t be all that hard to accomplish. Israel has already demonstrated that, albeit with human agency at the helm. The dismissal of the documentary NAZA, which scored an unprecedented standing ovation and a Special Jury Prize in Venice last week, as a “blood libel”, is a typical Nazi-like response. What might be seen as critical mass for AI comes at a time when global politics are in disarray. Like all emerging technologies in previous centuries, the human value of AI depends on how it is deployed. It can serve as a tremendously useful tool, provided its destructive capacities are constrained. But what are the chances of that in a realm where Trump and his acolytes rule the roost? Long before the advent of the internet, there were warnings from prescient scientists. Losing all hope could be premature. But, frequently through human existence, hoping for the best and preparing for the worst has been the least disastrous option. Let’s stick with it for the time being.
articles.author: Mahir Ali

articles.title: Schools and smog
articles.content: AFTER a three-month summer break, Lahore’s school gates officially reopened on Aug 24, bringing back the hurried footsteps of children racing to beat the morning bell and bursts of laughter as they spill through the school gates in the afternoon. With them have come pickups and rickshaws, bulging with children and their oversized schoolbags, motorcycles weaving through traffic, often carrying three or more students at a time, and cars — so many cars — streaming across the city, sometimes carrying just one child. Buses carrying 20 or more children, meanwhile, are a rare sight. Undoubtedly, beneath the bustle of the daily school run lies the palpable innocence of childhood — as well as the uneasy reality of the world they are growing up in. The cars, motorcycles and rickshaws ferrying children to and from school add to smoke that, come autumn, will mingle with dust, and turn the skies grey with smog. To mitigate the harm of the annual smog, the Punjab government announced the Pre-Smog Action Plan 2026 (July-September 2026), to “ensure timely preparedness, prevention and mitigation of smog during the upcoming smog season”. Broadly, and rightly, the action plan calls for stronger Environment Protection Agency monitoring, drone surveillance and activation of district anti-smog committees, alongside weekly coordination among relevant departments. It requires calibration of air quality monitors and emission testing stations, inspections of industries and brick kilns, and checks on construction sites and stone crushers. Transport measures include vehicle testing and action against vehicles emitting black smoke, among other critical measures. The plan largely carries forward the 10-year smog policy launched in 2024. To be fair, Lahore’s pollution levels were lower in 2025 than before — although favourable weather conditions had a hand in that improvement. But it is time to discuss measures that have escaped the smog plan’s purview so far — starting with the school traffic system. Lahore must revamp its school transport system. Lahore needs a transport system that puts hundreds of thousands of schoolchildren on far fewer vehicles. The government has attempted this, at its familiar slow pace, but only after pressure from the courts. In an Aug 13, 2026, judgement, Justice Shahid Karim of the Lahore High Court (LHC) noted that vehicular emissions account for 45 per cent of Lahore’s pollution, thus getting children into buses is about cutting emissions that contribute to dangerous smog. Justice Karim described the order as the “last judgement in the trilogy”, which arose from a petition filed in 2018 regarding environmental degradation in Punjab. Over eight years of proceedings, school transport became one strand of the case. The provincial government was directed to press schoolsto shift children from private vehicles to buses, to ensure buses for at least half the students, and to make transport compliance a condition of school registration. All these years, the government’s response to the court’s order has largely consisted of meetings with school administrations and associations, followed by letters urging compliance. It has been a token effort — for, the government has not pushed hard enough to persuade private schools to set aside their claims of limited resources and invest in buses. Off the record, private school officials say the government sends letters and raises school transport in meetings, but no one seriously expects anything to come of it. Lahore has hardly been a city of school buses. Since the mid-2000s, school transport has been shadowed by security concerns. During the years of the ‘war on terror’, when schools were conspicuous targets, parents saw buses carrying many children as a security risk. Then, in 2016, came a spate of reported child abductions across Punjab. In August that year, the then LHC chief justice Mansoor Ali Shah ordered schools to deploy security guards in pick-and-drop vans and directed the police to monitor school transport. The fear was not confined to kidnapping. The rape and murder of Zainab Ansari in Kasur in 2018 intensified a wider anxiety about children’s vulnerability — and about the adults entrusted with their care. Then there was the danger posed by the vehicles themselves, with children often sharing space with unsafe gas cylinders. To say that those fears have disappeared would be incorrect. They persist. And the urgency to overcome them has grown. The number of vehicles making the journey twice a day must be reduced. The stress on educating children rings hollow if the air they inhale is dangerous to their health. The best solution, of course, is a public school bus system — unless schools are brought within walking distance of every child. The writer is a freelance journalist based in Lahore.
articles.author: Alefia T. Hussain

articles.title: Politics and protests
articles.content: IT is the same tired play. As soon as the opposition announces a protest, the government reflexively cracks down. Citizens are roughed up and arrested, and the security officials who round them up later collect medals for their services. There are no consequences for this abuse of state power. Indeed, it increasingly appears that the lead-up to a protest, and not the protest itself, is where the real political battle is fought. And all this is playing out at the moment on television screens and social media, as the PTIprepares for its Sept 27 march on Islamabadto demand its jailed founder’s release. The machinery of the state has kicked into action all over the country, armed with the usual pretexts of ‘prevention of violence’ and ‘protection of public infrastructure and property’. The actions taken to thwart the march appear to be many. At least 155, perhaps more, preventive detention orders have been issued under the MPO; lists have been drawn up of PTI leaders and workers for further ‘preventive arrests’; police personnel’s leaves have been cancelled;containers and roadblocks are being prepared; restrictions have been placed on rallies and public gatherings; andSection 144 has been implemented in Punjab, with plans of a broader rollout soon. Authorities undoubtedly have a responsibility to maintain order, and reasonable measures to discharge that responsibility are legitimate. But half a dozen overlapping instruments, deployed against a political party’s leadership and rank and file, cannot be considered reasonable by any stretch. Sadly, such actions only give the impression that even calls for protest are considered a thought crime in our society. The heavy-handedness with which the government has been curtailing the opposition’s ability to exercise its lawful political rights should not be overlooked. Every democracy allows its citizens to express their will in different ways, including through peaceful public protests. That the government can and will prosecute political leaders and workers who actually break the law is not in dispute; the state has every right to respond firmly when violent protest tactics are employed deliberately. However, the point is that deterrents already exist and do not require the pre-emptive detention of people who have broken no law. Past protests may have turned violent, but that history cannot be used as a justification to arbitrarily suspend constitutional rights for those who have caused no offence. It is time to stop treating dissent as a security threat and allow the public a peaceful outlet to air its grievances. The consequences of not ceding that space gracefully will only grow more severe with time. A government confident in its own legitimacy does not need to criminalise the mere anticipation of a protest. Ours, evidently, is not that confident.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Prudent move
articles.content: THE State Bank’s decision to hold the policy rate at 11.5pc is the right one. With seven of the 10 members voting for the status quo, the Monetary Policy Committee has, with reason, resisted the wider business pressure — and temptation — to revert to monetary policy easing in an uncertain global economic environment exacerbated by the war in the Middle East. The case for a pause is even stronger today than it was a few months ago despite external sector stability and improved macroeconomic fundamentals. These are encouraging developments for an economy that has repeatedly been constrained by its external account. But the improvement should not be mistaken for the end of the crisis. The regional situation that appeared to be moving towards resolution a few weeks ago now looks uncertain. Oil supplies remain vulnerable to disruptions while uncertainty over shipping, energy routes and regional security continues. For an import-dependent economy such as Pakistan, a renewed oil shock could quickly widen the import bill, push inflation higher and put pressure on the rupee. The latest inflation numbers underline that risk. Headline inflation accelerated sharply to 11.1pc in August from 9.2pc in July, showing how quickly supply-side pressures can return. The SBP acknowledges that inflation risks have risen significantly. This makes monetary policy particularly difficult. Cutting rates now would hardly provide any support to investment and domestic demand. Rather, it would risk adding to external and inflationary pressures if the regional shock intensifies. How inflation and interest rates move in the coming months will largely be determined by energy prices and the duration of the regional disruption. A premature rate cut is not necessary to achieve the modest growth recovery of 3.5-4.5pc, particularly when monetary conditions have already eased substantially from their previous punishing levels. For now, therefore, the continuation of the pause is desirable. The economy has gained some breathing space, but the external environment remains too uncertain for a rate cut. The central bank should preserve its room to respond if the regional crisis produces another oil or balance-of-payment shock. Instead of demanding lower rates at this moment, the business community should be calling for real reforms: the ones required to broaden the tax net, fix the energy sector, ensure policy predictability and improve export competitiveness.
articles.author: Editorial
